To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) a causal rate distortion function for a Markov source can be computed in a simple manner for a two-channel system, (b) an upper bound on the rate that can be conveyed to the scheduler is obtained by an algorithmic approach, and (c) the gap between the entropic and causal rate distortion functions can be computed in the case of two-channel system.
the causal rate distortion is a fundamental performance measure of an opportunistic communication scheme and that the rate distortion function can be computed in closed form.

the rate at which channel state information must to be conveyed to the scheduler increases with the number of channels, the number of states of each channel, and the channel state information quality.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: How much channel state information must the transmitter know to meet an expected throughput constraint?
the problem of scheduling transmissions over multiple channels, based on limited channel state information.
the fundamental trade-off between the amount of channel state information available at the transmitter and the resulting throughput.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the causal information rate-distortion is a more appropriate metric than causal entropic rate distortion in characterizing the fundamental limits of opportunistic communication.
the causal information rate-distortion function is a lower bound on the causal entropic-rate-distortion function.
we characterize a fundamental limit of the amount of causal channel state information required to meet a throughput constraint.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the causal information rate-distortion function provides the tightest lower bound on the rate that CSI must be communicated to the transmitter in an opportunistic system.

, in order to achieve a given expected throughput, a transmitter requires less channel state information if the channel state information is encoded in a causal manner than if it is encoded in a noncausal manner.
the causal information rate-distortion function can be computed exactly, and the causal entropies can be used as a good approximation for it.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the causal information rate-distortion function is strictly less than the causal entropic information rate distortion function.

the rate distortion approach can be used to characterize a fundamental limit of channel state information in opportunistic scheduling, and that the distortion metric we propose is a natural metric capturing the impact on expected throughput of imperfect knowledge of the network channel state.

the amount of channel state information required by a transmitter to meet a constraint in expected throughput is significantly smaller than the amount of state information that must be conveyed to achieve the optimal expected throughput.
